language.script_notes: Portuguese uses ã/õ nasal tildes and ç, distinguishing it at a glance from Spanish. Street signs read 'Rua', 'Avenida', 'Estrada', 'Praça', 'Rotunda' — all different words from Spanish equivalents ('Calle', 'Avenida', 'Carretera', 'Plaza', 'Rotonda').

road_furniture.bollard_color: White with either a thin white top (wedge-shaped) or a wide flat reflector; a duller orange reflector variant also occurs, noticeably darker/less saturated than Spain's yellow reflectors.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Wedge-shaped or flat-topped posts, distinct from Spain's more rounded style.
road_furniture.line_paint: Center/edge line combinations mixing yellow and white segments in patterns distinct from Spain's more uniform white lines.
road_furniture.curb_style: Traditional black-and-white (or beige-and-white) calçada portuguesa mosaic cobblestone pavement in historic town centers and sidewalks — a strong, near-unique Portugal tell.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Portugal-specific curve/chevron/roundabout/pedestrian-crossing sign designs, distinct in style from Spain's equivalents. Galp is the dominant fuel station brand, vs. Repsol/Cepsa in Spain.

architecture.roof_style: Simple pitched roofs on whitewashed houses; red tile roofs nationwide.
architecture.roof_material: Terracotta barrel tile roofing is standard nationwide.
architecture.wall_construction: Whitewashed masonry walls are the classic Portuguese look, frequently covered in blue-and-white azulejo ceramic tiles on building façades — Portugal covers entire building exteriors in tile far more extensively than Spain does.
architecture.wall_color_palette: White walls with blue-and-white (cobalt) azulejo tile patterns is the single strongest Portugal architectural tell; colourful painted townhouses in Lisbon/Porto.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Azulejo-tiled townhouse façades; whitewashed Algarve village houses with chimney-pot decoration; steep tiled-roof Porto riverside houses; windmills in rural areas.

nature.vegetation: Cork oak and holm oak savanna-like 'montado' woodland across the southern Alentejo plains; terraced vineyards along the Douro Valley; pine and eucalyptus forest in the center/north; olive groves throughout.
nature.terrain: Atlantic coastline running the length of the country; rolling hills and mountains in the north (Peneda-Gerês); flatter wheat/cork plains in the Alentejo south; terraced river valleys (Douro).
nature.climate_signature: Mediterranean/Atlantic climate — greener and cooler in the north, drier and more golden in the Alentejo south; bright coastal light along the Algarve.

vehicles.plate_color: White plate with a blue EU strip on the left. Older plates (pre-2020) also carry a distinctive yellow strip on the right showing the registration month/year — Portugal is the only European country pairing a blue left strip with a yellow right strip. Newer plates (post-2020) drop the yellow strip and look closer to the general EU standard.
vehicles.plate_format: AA-NN-NN or similar letter/digit groupings depending on registration era.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Standard Western European fleet; smaller cars and vans proportionally more common than in wealthier neighbours.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Mostly Gen 3, some Gen 4 in cities.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Good coverage along the coast and main routes; thinner in the remote interior/mountainous north.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Iberian Peninsula, similar Mediterranean/Atlantic climate and terrain, similar Latin-derived language at a glance
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Portuguese has ã/õ nasal tildes and ç absent from Spanish spelling; Portugal's blue-and-white azulejo-tiled building façades are far more extensive than Spain's; Portuguese plates historically carry the yellow right-hand strip Spain's plates lack; calçada mosaic pavement is a strong Portugal-only tell.

Brazil drives on the right with very different tropical vegetation, yellow-plate-then-Mercosul plates, and a totally different, generally lower-density built environment than Portugal's dense whitewashed European towns.
